# Erdős Problem 344, the $\sqrt{2N}$ variant

*Generated by an AI agent and machine-checked (Lean file `Erdos344.lean`); not reviewed by a human expert.*

**In words.** If a set of natural numbers has at least $\sqrt{2N}$ elements up to $N$, for every large $N$, then the sums of
distinct elements of the set contain an infinite arithmetic progression. This is a variant of Erdős Problem 344. The headline
problem asks for the same conclusion when the set has at least $K\sqrt N$ elements up to $N$, for some absolute constant $K$; it was
solved long ago (Szemerédi and Vu 2006; see also Chen 2003). No constant below $\sqrt2$ would do: for every $c<\sqrt2$, having at
least $c\sqrt N$ elements up to every large $N$ does not suffice (a remark of Erdős, 1961/62; see Remark 2, not formalized).

**Theorem.** *Let $A\subseteq\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ and let $N_0$ be a natural number such that
$|A\cap\{1,\dots,N\}|\ge\sqrt{2N}$ for all $N\ge N_0$. Then there are integers $x\ge0$ and $d\ge1$ such that for every integer
$k\ge0$ the number $x+kd$ is a sum of finitely many distinct elements of $A$.* (The empty sum $0$ is allowed. This matters only if
$x=0$, and then one may replace $x$ by $d$.)

**Idea.** List $A$ as $a_0<a_1<\cdots$; the hypothesis gives $a_m\le m^2/2+1$ for large $m$. Call a part of $A$ good if each of its
elements exceeds the sum of the smaller elements of that part by at most a constant. The sums of distinct elements of an infinite
good part have bounded gaps. So it is enough to find arbitrarily long progressions, with one fixed difference $d$, among the sums of
elements outside this part.

*Case 1: some difference $a_{i+1}-a_i=d$ occurs infinitely often.* Take a very sparse family of such pairs. Choosing one element
from each pair gives progressions with difference $d$. The rest of $A$ is good. Indeed, if $a_{i+1}=a_i+1$ for all large $i$, there
is nothing to prove. Otherwise $a_i\ge i+4$ for large $i$. The numbers $i+4$, $i<m$, add up to $m^2/2+7m/2$, and the sparse pairs
take away at most $3m+O(1)$ of this. So the remaining elements before $a_m$ add up to at least $m^2/2-O(1)\ge a_m-O(1)$. Only here
is the constant $\sqrt2$ needed: Case 2 would work with any bound $a_m=O(m^2)$ and a larger number in place of $11$ (the text and
the Lean file use the bound above).

*Case 2: $a_{i+1}\ge a_i+11$ for all large $i$.* Then each of the four residue classes of indices modulo $4$ gives a good part of
$A$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the sets of all sums of distinct elements of the first part and of the second part; their gaps are at most
some number $G$. Let $b_0<b_1<\cdots$ be the third part. The fourth is the good part needed at the end. We look for long progressions
among the sums of an element of $X$, an element of $Y$ and some distinct $b_i$. The numbers $n,d,L,m,R,D$ below are fixed in this
order, and each may depend on those before it ($L$ is given).

Start with $Z_0=X\cap[0,(G+1)R)$, which has at least $R$ elements, and add the $b_i$ one by one: $Z_{i+1}=Z_i\cup(Z_i+b_i)$. For
fixed $i$, $Z_i$ lies below $(G+1)R+O_i(1)$. So $|Z_i|/R$ is at most about $G+1$ for large $R$, and it cannot go up by a fixed
amount again and again. Hence for a given $\varepsilon>0$ there is an $n$ such that for every $m\ge n$ some $R$ makes
$|Z_m|-|Z_n|<\varepsilon R$. As $b_i=O(i^2)$, there is a $\kappa$ with $8b_i\le\kappa s^2$ for all $s$ and all $i<2s$. Take such an
$n$ for a small $\varepsilon$ depending only on $G$ and $\kappa$, and put $d=(\kappa n)!$. Now let $L$ be the length wanted. Take a
suitable large $m$, and then $R$ as above.

Among the $b_i$ with $n\le i<2n$ for which $|Z_{i+1}|-|Z_i|$ is small, two differ by a number $D<\kappa n$, by the pigeonhole
principle. If $x$ is not too large, $z+xD\in Z_{2n}$ for most $z\in Z_n$. The same argument at the scales
$4\kappa n,(4\kappa)^2n,\dots,m/2$, with two $b_i$ whose difference is a multiple of $D$, extends this to larger $x$: for every
integer $0\le x\le m$ fewer than $|Z_n|/(G+1)$ of the $z\in Z_n$ have $z+xD\notin Z_m$. As $D$ divides $d$, the shifts $jd$,
$0\le j\le L$, are of the form $xD$ with $0\le x\le m$. Finally, some number $t$ has at least $|Z_n|/(G+1)$ representations $t=y+z$
with $y\in Y$, $z\in Z_n$. For each $j\le L$ one of them has $z+jd\in Z_m$, and so $t+jd=y+(z+jd)$ is in $Y+Z_m$.

## 1. Enumeration and gluing

**Lemma 1.** *$A$ is infinite, and if $a_0<a_1<a_2<\cdots$ are its elements, then $2a_k\le k^2+2$ for all large $k$.*

*Proof.* If $A$ were finite, $|A\cap\{1,\dots,N\}|\le|A|<\sqrt{2N}$ for large $N$. Let $k\ge N_0+1$ and $N=a_k-1$. Since
$a_k\ge k$, we have $N\ge N_0$. The elements of $A$ in $\{1,\dots,N\}$ are among $a_0,\dots,a_{k-1}$, so
$\sqrt{2(a_k-1)}\le k$. $\square$

**From now on $a_0<a_1<\cdots$ is a fixed sequence of natural numbers with $2a_k\le k^2+2$ for all large $k$.** By Lemma 1 the
elements of $A$ form such a sequence. Note that $a_i\ge i$. The letters $J,J',B,C,F$ denote sets of indices, that is, subsets of
$\mathbb N$. For a set $J$ of indices let

* $P(J)$ be the set of all sums $\sum_{i\in T}a_i$, where $T\subseteq J$ is finite (the empty sum $0$ is allowed);
* $S_J(m)=\sum_{i\in J,\ i<m}a_i$.

In particular, $P(\mathbb N)$ is the set of all sums of finitely many distinct terms of the sequence. If $J\subseteq J'$, then
$P(J)\subseteq P(J')$. If $J\cap J'=\emptyset$, then $P(J)+P(J')\subseteq P(J\cup J')$. The set $J$ is **$G$-good** if
$a_m\le G+S_J(m)$ for every $m\in J$, and **good** if it is $G$-good for some natural number $G$. A set $X\subseteq\mathbb N$ is
**$G$-syndetic** if for every $u\in\mathbb N$ there is $x\in X$ with $x\le u\le x+G$, and **syndetic** if it is $G$-syndetic for
some natural number $G$. A **progression with difference $d$** has the terms $x,x+d,x+2d,\dots$, finitely or infinitely many, where
$x\ge0$ and $d\ge1$ are integers.

**Lemma 2 (bounded gaps).** *If $C$ is infinite and $G$-good, then $P(C)$ is $G$-syndetic.*

*Proof.* We show by induction on $m$: for every natural number $u\le G+S_C(m)$ there is $c\in P(C\cap[0,m))$ with $c\le u\le c+G$.
For $m=0$ take $c=0$. Step from $m$ to $m+1$: if $m\notin C$ or $u\le G+S_C(m)$, use the statement for $m$. Otherwise $m\in C$ and
$G+S_C(m)<u\le G+S_C(m)+a_m$. As $C$ is $G$-good, $a_m\le G+S_C(m)<u$. So $u-a_m$ is a natural number $\le G+S_C(m)$; take $c'$ for
$u-a_m$ and put $c=c'+a_m$.

Given any $u\in\mathbb N$, choose $m\in C$ with $m>u$. Then $S_C(m+1)\ge a_m\ge m>u$, and the statement for $m+1$ applies. $\square$

**Lemma 3 (multiples of $d$).** *If $C$ is infinite and good and $d\ge1$, then the multiples of $d$ in $P(C)$ form a
syndetic set.*

*Proof.* Let $H$ be the set of residues modulo $d$ of the elements of $P(C)$. For each $h\in H$ choose a finite subset of $C$ whose
sum has the residue $h$. Let $F\subseteq C$ be the union of these finitely many sets. Then every $h\in H$ is the residue of some
element of $P(F)$.

*Every $c\in P(C\setminus F)$ has some $f\in P(F)$ with $d\mid f+c$.* Indeed, $h\mapsto h+c$ maps $H$ into itself, because $h$ is
the residue of some $f\in P(F)$ and $f+c\in P(C)$. This map is injective and $H$ is finite, so it is onto. As $0\in H$ (the empty
sum), some $h\in H$ has $h+c\equiv0\pmod d$, and $h$ is the residue of some $f\in P(F)$.

Let $C$ be $G$-good and $\sigma=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$. For $m\in C\setminus F$ we have
$a_m\le G+S_C(m)\le G+\sigma+S_{C\setminus F}(m)$, so $C\setminus F$ is $(G+\sigma)$-good; it is also infinite. Let
$u\in\mathbb N$. If $u<\sigma$, then $0$ is a multiple of $d$ in $P(C)$ with $0\le u\le 0+\sigma$. If $u\ge\sigma$,
Lemma 2 gives $c\in P(C\setminus F)$ with $c\le u-\sigma\le c+G+\sigma$. With $f$ as above, $f+c$ is a multiple of $d$
in $P(C)$, and since $0\le f\le\sigma$ we get $f+c\le u\le (f+c)+G+2\sigma$. $\square$

**Lemma 4 (gluing).** *Let $J$ and $C$ be disjoint, $C$ infinite and good, and $d\ge1$. Suppose that for every $L$ there is
$x$ such that $x,x+d,\dots,x+Ld$ all lie in $P(J)$. Then $P(J\cup C)$ contains an infinite progression with difference
$d$.*

*Proof.* By Lemma 3 the multiples of $d$ in $P(C)$ form a $\Gamma$-syndetic set for some $\Gamma$. Take $x$ for $L=\Gamma$.
For $k\ge0$ there is $c\in P(C)$ with $d\mid c$ and $c\le kd\le c+\Gamma$. So $kd-c=jd$ with $0\le j\le\Gamma$, and
$x+kd=(x+jd)+c\in P(J)+P(C)$. $\square$

## 2. Case 1: some difference $a_{i+1}-a_i$ occurs infinitely often

**Lemma 5.** *If $a_{i+1}\ne a_i+1$ for infinitely many $i$, then $a_i-i\to\infty$.*

*Proof.* The integers $a_i-i$ are nondecreasing, and they increase at each such $i$. $\square$

Let $d\ge1$ be such that $a_{i+1}=a_i+d$ for infinitely many $i$. Choose indices $p_0,p_1,\dots$ among these $i$ with
$$p_{r+1}\ge 3p_r+9\qquad(r\ge0),$$
and let $B=\{p_0,p_0+1,\ p_1,p_1+1,\ \dots\}$. The pairs $\{p_r,p_r+1\}$ are disjoint, and the complement $C$ of $B$ is infinite, since
it contains all $p_r+2$.

**Lemma 6.** *(a) Let $W(m)=\sum_{i\in B,\ i<m}(i+4)$. Then $W(m)\le 3m+6$ for all $m$, and $W(m)\le p_r$ whenever $m\le p_r$.
(b) For every $L$ there is $x$ such that $x,x+d,\dots,x+Ld$ all lie in $P(B)$.*

*Proof.* (a) We show by induction on $r$ that both bounds hold for all $m\le p_r$. For $r=0$ we have $W(m)=0$. Step from $r$ to
$r+1$: let $p_r<m\le p_{r+1}$. No element of $B$ lies in $[p_r+2,m)$, and $W(p_r)\le p_r$, so
$$W(m)\le W(p_r)+(p_r+4)+(p_r+5)\le3p_r+9,$$
which is at most $3m+6$ and at most $p_{r+1}$.

(b) Let $x=\sum_{r<L}a_{p_r}$. For $0\le j\le L$,
$$x+jd=\sum_{r<j}a_{p_r+1}+\sum_{j\le r<L}a_{p_r},$$
and the indices on the right are distinct elements of $B$. $\square$

**Lemma 7.** *If $a_k\ge k+4$ for all large $k$, then $C$ is good.*

*Proof.* Choose $k_0$ such that $2a_k\le k^2+2$ and $a_k\ge k+4$ for all $k\ge k_0$. Let $w=\sum_{i<k_0}(i+4)$ and
$G=a_{k_0}+w+7$. Let $m\in C$. If $m<k_0$, then $a_m\le a_{k_0}\le G$. Let $m\ge k_0$. Since $i+4\le a_i$ for $i\ge k_0$, and since
$\sum_{i<m}(i+4)=(m^2+7m)/2$,
$$S_C(m)+w\ \ge\sum_{i\in C,\ i<m}(i+4)=\frac{m^2+7m}2-W(m)\ \ge\ \frac{m^2+7m}2-(3m+6)\ \ge\ \frac{m^2}2-6\ \ge\ a_m-7.$$
So $a_m\le G+S_C(m)$. $\square$

**Proposition 8 (Case 1).** *If $a_{i+1}=a_i+d$ for infinitely many $i$, then $P(\mathbb N)$ contains an infinite progression.*

*Proof.* If $a_{i+1}=a_i+1$ for all large $i$, the numbers $a_i$ themselves contain one. Otherwise $a_k\ge k+4$ for all large
$k$ by Lemma 5, so $C$ is good by Lemma 7. Now Lemma 6(b) and Lemma 4 with $J=B$ give the claim. $\square$

## 3. Shifts with small loss

For finite sets $Z,Z'$ of integers and an integer $v$, the **loss** is
$$\lambda(Z,Z';v)=|(Z+v)\setminus Z'|=\#\{z\in Z:\ z+v\notin Z'\}.$$

**Lemma 9.** *Let $Z,Z',Z'',U,U'$ be finite sets of integers and $v,w$ integers.*
*(a) If $U\subseteq Z$ and $Z'\subseteq U'$, then $\lambda(U,U';v)\le\lambda(Z,Z';v)$.*
*(b) $\lambda(Z,Z'';v+w)\le\lambda(Z,Z';v)+\lambda(Z',Z'';w)$.*
*(c) $\lambda(Z,Z;-v)=\lambda(Z,Z;v)$.*
*(d) $\lambda(Z,Z;xv)\le x\,\lambda(Z,Z;v)$ for integers $x\ge0$.*

*Proof.* (a) is clear. (b) If $z\in Z$ and $z+v+w\notin Z''$, then either $z+v\notin Z'$, or $z'=z+v$ is an element of $Z'$
with $z'+w\notin Z''$. (c) The map $z\mapsto z+v$ is a bijection from $\{z\in Z:z+v\in Z\}$ to $\{z\in Z:z-v\in Z\}$, so
the complements of these two sets in $Z$ have equal size. (d) is clear for $x=0$; use (b) and induction on $x$. $\square$

Now let $b_0<b_1<\cdots$ be natural numbers. For a finite set $Z$ of integers put
$$Z_0=Z,\qquad Z_{i+1}=Z_i\cup(Z_i+b_i),\qquad \delta_i=|Z_{i+1}|-|Z_i|=\lambda(Z_i,Z_i;b_i).$$

**Lemma 10.** *(a) $\sum_{s\le i<m}\delta_i=|Z_m|-|Z_s|$ for $s\le m$. (b) If $s\le q\le p\le m$ and $x\ge0$ is an integer, then
$\lambda(Z_s,Z_m;x(b_p-b_q))\le x(\delta_q+\delta_p)$.*

*Proof.* (a) is clear. (b) By Lemma 9(b) and (a), then (d) and (c),
$$\lambda(Z_s,Z_m;-xb_q+xb_p)\le\lambda(Z_s,Z_p;-xb_q)+\lambda(Z_p,Z_m;xb_p)\le\lambda(Z_q,Z_q;-xb_q)+\lambda(Z_p,Z_p;xb_p)
\le x\delta_q+x\delta_p.\ \square$$

## 4. One block and all scales

Let $b_0<b_1<\cdots$ be natural numbers as above. From here to Proposition 15, $\kappa\ge1$ is an integer such that
$$8b_i\le\kappa s^2\qquad\text{for all integers } s\ge0\text{ and }0\le i<2s. \tag{1}$$
(If $G\ge1$ is an integer and $b_i\le G(i+1)^2$ for all $i$, then $8b_i\le8G(2s)^2$ for $i<2s$, so $\kappa=32G$ has this property.)
The number $\kappa$ depends only on the sequence $b_0,b_1,\dots$. Lemmas 11 and 12 hold for every finite set $Z$ of integers, with
$Z_i$ as in Section 3. The numbers $v$ and $D$ which they give may depend on $Z$.

**Lemma 11 (one block).** *Let $D\ge1$ and $s\ge4D$ be integers. There is an integer $v$ with $0<v<\kappa s$ such that for all
integers $0\le x\le4\kappa^2s$*
$$\lambda(Z_s,Z_{2s};\,x\,vD)\le16\kappa^2\,(|Z_{2s}|-|Z_s|).$$

*Proof.* Let $\Delta=|Z_{2s}|-|Z_s|=\sum_{s\le i<2s}\delta_i$. Call $i\in[s,2s)$ *cheap* if $s\delta_i\le2\Delta$. More than half of
these $s$ indices are cheap. Otherwise $s\delta_i>2\Delta$ for at least $s/2>0$ of them, and the sum of these $s\delta_i$ is greater
than $\frac s2\cdot2\Delta=s\Delta$; but the sum of all the $s\delta_i$ is $s\Delta$.

Let $w=\kappa sD$. For $i\in[s,2s)$ we have $\lfloor b_i/w\rfloor\le\kappa s^2/(8w)=s/(8D)$ by (1). So the pair
$(b_i\bmod D,\ \lfloor b_i/w\rfloor)$ takes at most $D\left(\frac s{8D}+1\right)=\frac s8+D\le\frac{3s}8<\frac s2$ values, and two
cheap indices $q<p$ have the same pair. Then $D\mid b_p-b_q$ and $0<b_p-b_q<w$, so $b_p-b_q=vD$ with $0<v<\kappa s$. By Lemma
10(b) the loss in question is at most $x(\delta_q+\delta_p)\le4\kappa^2s\cdot\frac{4\Delta}s=16\kappa^2\Delta$. $\square$

**Lemma 12 (all scales).** *Let $n\ge4$ be an integer and $s_k=(4\kappa)^kn$. There is an integer $D$ with $0<D<\kappa n$ such that for
all $k\ge0$ and all integers $0\le x\le4\kappa^2s_k$*
$$\lambda(Z_n,Z_{2s_k};\,xD)\le16\kappa^2\,(|Z_{2s_k}|-|Z_n|).$$

*Proof.* Apply Lemma 11 with $1$ in place of $D$ and with $s=n$, and call the number it gives $D$. Then $0<D<\kappa n$, and the case
$k=0$ holds. Suppose the claim holds for $k$, and let $0\le x\le4\kappa^2s_{k+1}$. As $s_{k+1}\ge4\kappa n>4D$, Lemma 11 applies
with $D$ and $s=s_{k+1}$; let $v$ be the number it gives, $0<v<\kappa s_{k+1}=4\kappa^2s_k$. Write $x=x'+x''v$ with
$0\le x'<v$ and $x''\ge 0$. Then $x'\le4\kappa^2s_k$ and $x''\le x\le4\kappa^2s_{k+1}$. Since $2s_k\le s_{k+1}$, Lemma 9(b),(a), the
case $k$ and Lemma 11 give
$$\begin{aligned}\lambda(Z_n,Z_{2s_{k+1}};xD)&\le\lambda(Z_n,Z_{2s_k};x'D)+\lambda(Z_{s_{k+1}},Z_{2s_{k+1}};x''\,vD)\\
&\le16\kappa^2\left(|Z_{2s_k}|-|Z_n|+|Z_{2s_{k+1}}|-|Z_{s_{k+1}}|\right)\le16\kappa^2\left(|Z_{2s_{k+1}}|-|Z_n|\right).\ \square\end{aligned}$$

## 5. The key proposition

**Lemma 13 (saturation).** *For $i,R\ge0$ let $\varphi_i(R)$ be natural numbers with $\varphi_i(R)\le gR+c_i$, where $g$ and
the $c_i$ are natural numbers. For all natural numbers $M,n_0$ there is $n\ge n_0$ such that for every $m\ge n$ there is
some $R$ with $M(\varphi_m(R)-\varphi_n(R))<R$.*

*Proof.* Otherwise for every $n\ge n_0$ there is $m\ge n$ with $M\varphi_m(R)\ge M\varphi_n(R)+R$ for all $R$. Starting at $n_0$
and repeating this $r$ times, we find $m$ with $M\varphi_m(R)\ge rR$ for all $R$. For $r=M(g+1)+1$ and $R=c_m+1$ this says
$rR\le M(gR+c_m)\le M(g+1)R<rR$, a contradiction. $\square$

**Lemma 14 (popular sum).** *Let $Y$ be $G$-syndetic, and let $Z,Z'$ be finite sets of integers, where $Z$ has no negative elements
and $(G+1)\ell<|Z|$ for an integer $\ell\ge0$. There is a natural number $t$ such that $t+v\in Y+Z'$ for every integer $v$ with
$\lambda(Z,Z';v)\le\ell$.*

*Proof.* Let $u$ be a natural number with $z\le u$ for all $z\in Z$. For $z\in Z$ there is $y_z\in Y$ with
$y_z\le u+G-z\le y_z+G$, so $z+y_z\in[u,u+G]$. This interval contains $G+1$ integers, so some $t$ in it equals $z+y_z$ for more than
$\ell$ elements $z\in Z$. If $\lambda(Z,Z';v)\le\ell$, one of these $z$ has $z+v\in Z'$, and $t+v=y_z+(z+v)$. $\square$

Let $\Sigma(b)$ be the set of all sums $\sum_{i\in T}b_i$ over finite sets $T$ of indices.

**Proposition 15 (key proposition).** *Let $X,Y\subseteq\mathbb N$ be $G$-syndetic, and let $b_0<b_1<\cdots$ be natural numbers
satisfying (1). There is $d\ge1$ such that for every $L$ there is $t$ with $t+jd\in X+Y+\Sigma(b)$ for all $0\le j\le L$.*

*Proof.* *The starting sets.* For $R\ge0$ let $Z(R)=X\cap[0,(G+1)R)$. Each of the intervals $[j(G+1),\,j(G+1)+G]$, $0\le j<R$,
contains an element of $X$, so $|Z(R)|\ge R$. Let $Z_i(R)$, $i\ge0$, be the sets obtained from $Z=Z(R)$ as in Section 3. Every
element of $Z_i(R)$ is an element of $Z(R)$ plus a sum of distinct terms among $b_0,\dots,b_{i-1}$. Hence
$Z_i(R)\subseteq X+\Sigma(b)$ and $|Z_i(R)|\le(G+1)R+b_0+\dots+b_{i-1}$.

*Choice of $n$ and $d$.* Apply Lemma 13 to $\varphi_i(R)=|Z_i(R)|$ with $M=(G+1)\cdot16\kappa^2$ and $n_0=4$. It gives $n\ge4$ such that
for every $m\ge n$ some $R$ satisfies
$$(G+1)\cdot16\kappa^2\left(|Z_m(R)|-|Z_n(R)|\right)<R. \tag{2}$$
Put $d=(\kappa n)!$.

*Conclusion.* Let $L\ge0$. Choose $k$ such that $s_k=(4\kappa)^kn$ is at least $Ld$ (for instance $k=Ld$), and put $s=s_k$ and
$m=2s$. Then $m\ge n$. Choose $R$ with (2), write $Z=Z(R)$, and let $\ell=16\kappa^2(|Z_m|-|Z_n|)$. By (2),
$(G+1)\ell<R\le|Z_0|\le|Z_n|$. Let $t$ be the number that Lemma 14 gives for $Y$, $Z_n$, $Z_m$ and $\ell$, and let $D$ be the number
that Lemma 12 gives for $Z$ and $n$. Since $0<D<\kappa n$, $D$ divides $d$. For $0\le j\le L$ we have $jd=xD$ with
$x=jd/D\le Ld\le s\le4\kappa^2s$. So Lemma 12 gives $\lambda(Z_n,Z_m;jd)\le\ell$. Therefore $t+jd\in Y+Z_m\subseteq Y+X+\Sigma(b)$.
The number $d$ does not depend on $L$. $\square$

## 6. Case 2: $a_{i+1}\ge a_i+11$ for all large $i$

**Lemma 16.** *(a) If $a_{i+1}\ge a_i+11$ for all large $i$, then $a_k\ge10k$ for all large $k$.*

*(b) Let $2a_k\le k^2+2$ and $a_k\ge10k$ for all $k\ge Q$, where $Q\ge1$, and let $G=8(Q+1)^2$. Let $0\le r\le3$ and
$J_r=\{4q+r:\ q\ge0\}$. Then $J_r$ is $G$-good, and $a_{4q+r}\le G(q+1)^2$ for all $q\ge0$.*

*Proof.* (a) Let $a_{i+1}\ge a_i+11$ for all $i\ge i_0$. Then $a_k\ge11(k-i_0)\ge10k$ for $k\ge11i_0$.

(b) For $q\ge Q$ we have $2a_{4q+r}\le(4q+3)^2+2\le16(q+1)^2$, that is,
$$a_{4q+r}\le8(q+1)^2. \tag{3}$$
For $q\le Q$, therefore, $a_{4q+r}\le a_{4Q+r}\le G$. In both cases $a_{4q+r}\le G(q+1)^2$. Next,
$$8(q+1)^2\le G+S_{J_r}(4q+r)\qquad(q\ge0). \tag{4}$$
This is clear for $q\le Q$. If it holds for some $q\ge Q$, it holds for $q+1$, because the right side increases by
$a_{4q+r}\ge40q\ge16q+24=8(q+2)^2-8(q+1)^2$. Now let $m=4q+r\in J_r$. If $q\le Q$, then $a_m\le G$; if $q\ge Q$, then
$a_m\le G+S_{J_r}(m)$ by (3) and (4). $\square$

**Proposition 17 (Case 2).** *If $a_k\ge10k$ for all large $k$, then $P(\mathbb N)$ contains an infinite progression.*

*Proof.* Choose $Q\ge1$ with $2a_k\le k^2+2$ and $a_k\ge10k$ for all $k\ge Q$, and let $G$ and $J_r$ be as in Lemma 16(b). The sets
$J_r$ are $G$-good. By Lemma 2, $X=P(J_0)$ and $Y=P(J_1)$ are $G$-syndetic. Let $b_q=a_{4q+2}$. As $b_q\le G(q+1)^2$, (1) holds with
$\kappa=32G$. By Proposition 15 there is $d\ge1$ such that $X+Y+\Sigma(b)\subseteq P(J_0\cup J_1\cup J_2)$ contains arbitrarily long
progressions with difference $d$. Apply Lemma 4 with $J=J_0\cup J_1\cup J_2$ and $C=J_3$. $\square$

**Proof of the Theorem.** By Lemma 1 we may apply the above to the elements $a_0<a_1<\cdots$ of $A$. If some $d\le10$ equals
$a_{i+1}-a_i$ for infinitely many $i$, use Proposition 8. Otherwise $a_{i+1}\ge a_i+11$ for all large $i$; use Lemma 16(a) and
Proposition 17. In both cases $P(\mathbb N)$, the set of sums of finitely many distinct elements of $A$, contains an infinite
progression. $\square$

## Two remarks (not part of the Lean file)

**Remark 1 (a slightly weaker hypothesis).** Let $c\ge0$ be an integer. If $a_0<a_1<\cdots$ are natural numbers with
$2a_k\le k^2+ck+2$ for all large $k$, then $P(\mathbb N)$ contains an infinite progression. The same proof works, with this bound in
place of $2a_k\le k^2+2$ everywhere (it is used in Lemmas 7 and 16(b) and in Propositions 8 and 17). Put $e=c+4$. Sections 3 to 5,
Lemmas 2 to 5 and Lemma 16(a) do not use the bound and stay as they are. The other changes are these.

* *Section 2.* Replace $i+4$ by $i+e$ (also in Lemma 7 and Proposition 8, where $a_k\ge k+4$ becomes $a_k\ge k+e$) and $3p_r+9$ by
  $3p_r+2e+1$ (in the choice of the $p_r$ and in Lemma 6(a), which becomes $W(m)\le3m+2e-2$). In Lemma 7,
  $\sum_{i<m}(i+e)=(m^2+(2c+7)m)/2$, the number $7$ in $G$ becomes $2e-1$, and the last chain ends with
  $\frac{m^2+(2c+7)m}2-(3m+2e-2)\ge\frac{m^2+cm}2+1-(2e-1)\ge a_m-(2e-1)$.
* *Section 6.* Replace $Q\ge1$ by $Q\ge1+c$, take $G=8(Q+1)^2+2c(Q+1)$, and replace $8(q+1)^2$ by $8(q+1)^2+2c(q+1)$ in (3) and (4).
  Here (3) holds because $(4q+3)^2+c(4q+3)+2\le16(q+1)^2+4c(q+1)$, the step for (4) is $40q\ge16q+24+2c$, and
  $8(q+1)^2+2c(q+1)\le G(q+1)^2$.

This includes Folkman's question below with his largest constant $\frac12$. His indices start at $1$ and ours at $0$. So his
$a_n\le\frac12n^2$ reads $2a_k\le(k+1)^2\le k^2+2k+2$ here, which is the case $c=2$. A copy of the Lean file with these changes
compiles, but it is not included in this repository and has not been reviewed. So $\sqrt{2N}$ is
not the exact threshold, which we do not determine.

**Remark 2 (no constant below $\sqrt2$ suffices).** Let $0<c<\sqrt2$. Choose indices $2\le k_1<k_2<\cdots$ with $k_1^2/c^2\ge k_1+1$
and $k_{j+1}\ge j\,k_j^2$. Let $a_i=i+1$ for $i<k_1$, let $a_{k_j}=\lfloor k_j^2/c^2\rfloor$ for $j\ge1$, and let $a_{i+1}=a_i+1$
for all other $i+1>k_1$.

If $k_j\le k\le k_{j+1}$, then $k^2-k_j^2=(k-k_j)(k+k_j)\ge c^2(k-k_j)$, so $a_{k_j}+(k-k_j)\le k^2/c^2$. For $k<k_{j+1}$ the left
side is $a_k$. Hence $a_k\le k^2/c^2$ for all $k\ge k_1$. For $k=k_{j+1}$ the left side is the integer $a_{k-1}+1$, so
$a_{k-1}+1\le a_k$. Also $a_{k_1-1}+1=k_1+1\le a_{k_1}$. So the sequence is strictly increasing. Let $N$ be large and
$k=\lfloor c\sqrt N\rfloor$. Then $a_0,\dots,a_k$ are in $\{1,\dots,N\}$, because $a_0=1$ and $a_k\le k^2/c^2\le N$. So the set
$A=\{a_0,a_1,\dots\}$ has at least $k+1\ge c\sqrt N$ elements in $\{1,\dots,N\}$.

Now let $k=k_{j+1}$. For $i<k$ we have $a_i\le i+k_j^2/c^2$, so the sum of $a_0,\dots,a_{k-1}$ is at most
$\frac{k^2}2+\frac{k\,k_j^2}{c^2}=(\frac12+o(1))k^2$ as $j\to\infty$, while $a_k=(c^{-2}+o(1))k^2$ with $c^{-2}>\frac12$. No element
of $P(\mathbb N)$ lies strictly between this sum and $a_k$. So $P(\mathbb N)$ has gaps of unbounded length and contains no infinite
progression.

## What is new and what is borrowed

*The statement.* Folkman [3, p. 655] asked: if $a_1<a_2<\cdots$ are natural numbers with $a_n\le\theta n^2$ for all large $n$, where
$\theta\le\frac12$ (he writes $M$), must the sums of distinct $a_n$ contain an infinite progression? By the Theorem, yes if
$\theta<\frac12$. Indeed, $\theta>0$ (as $a_n>0$ for $n\ge2$), and if $N$ is large, then $n=\lfloor\sqrt{N/\theta}\rfloor$ is large
and $a_1<\dots<a_n\le\theta n^2\le N$. At most one of these $n$ numbers is $0$, so at least $\lfloor\sqrt{N/\theta}\rfloor-1$ of
them lie in $\{1,\dots,N\}$, and for large $N$ this is at least $\sqrt{2N}$. (This deduction is on paper, not in Lean.) The case
$\theta=\frac12$ is not covered by the Theorem, only by Remark 1.

The Theorem is new as far as we know, so likely new, not certainly new. Two literature searches on 24 and 25 November 2026 found no
earlier proof, but they had gaps: we did not read the page and thread on the Erdős problems site, Section 6 of the Erdős–Graham
monograph (1980), Szemerédi's 2016 survey, and Fox and Knapp (2013); Google Scholar was not used, some database queries failed, and
the second search did not re-open [1] and [5]. The headline problem was solved by Szemerédi and Vu [6], and in a slightly weaker
form by Chen [5], after Erdős [1], Folkman [3], Hegyvári [4], and Łuczak and Schoen [10], who needed more elements. Chen's Theorem 1
says that for some $K>1$ it suffices that $|A\cap\{1,\dots,n\}|>K\sqrt n$ for all $n>K^2$. This threshold $K^2$ is the same for all
$A$, so formally his theorem is weaker than the version with "for all large $n$". (Szemerédi and Vu say that Chen also proved their
Theorem 9.4.) A Lean proof of the headline problem is in the GitHub repository `plby/lean-proofs`, file
`src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos344.lean`.

Two printed remarks conflict or may conflict with the Theorem. Hegyvári [4, p. 99] says, without proof, that it is easy to construct
a set $A$ with $|A\cap\{1,\dots,n\}|>\sqrt{2n}$ whose sums contain no infinite progression. If this is meant for all large $n$, it
contradicts the Theorem; it looks like a slip for $c\sqrt n$ with $c<\sqrt2$ (Remark 2). Chen [5, Section 4] writes that he
believes, without proof, that for every $K>0$ there is a set $A$ with $|A\cap\{1,\dots,n\}|\ge K\sqrt n$ for all large $n$ whose
sums contain no infinite progression. This conflicts with the Theorem, and already with [6, Corollary 1.4].

*The proof.* Lemma 2 is due to Graham [2] (see Burr and Erdős [7, Lemma 3.2]); Lemmas 3 and 4 are standard. The use of pairs in Case
1 is Lemma 6.1 of Fan [9] (partly inspired, as Fan says, by Lemma 5 of [2]). The lower bound for $S_C(m)$ in our Lemma 7 refines a
remark of Erdős [1, p. 346]: unless almost all differences are $1$, the sum of all $a_i$, $i<m$, exceeds $a_m$ by at least about
$\frac72m$. That this surplus, which comes from the constant $\sqrt2$, allows a sparse family of pairs to be removed was not found
by us in these papers. The plan of Case 2 (good parts give syndetic sets of sums, a third part moves by multiples of a fixed $d$,
one more good part finishes) is that of Bergelson and Simmons [8]. If the greatest common divisor of $\{a_i:i\ge m\}$ is the same
for all large $m$, Case 2 also follows from their Main Theorem 2.1 and a lemma on sequences of size $O(i^2)$. (This is a deduction
on paper. It was made for an earlier version of Case 2, with $a_k\ge100k$ and five index classes. It looks the same for the four
classes used here, but it was not redone in detail.) Sections 3 to 5, which need only counting and the pigeonhole principle, were
found by an AI agent for this proof. We know no source for Proposition 15, but no separate literature search was made for it. The
overall plan came from work on Erdős Problem 254; the agents that made it had read [9] and the Lean sources of Star Fleet Math's
`erdos-254` (in the GitHub repository `williamjblair/lean-proofs`) and of `plby/lean-proofs` on Problem 344, and used them for ideas
only. An expert could reasonably regard the whole as a modest assembly of known tools.

1. P. Erdős, *On the representation of large integers as sums of distinct summands taken from a fixed set*, Acta Arith. 7 (1961/62) 345–354.
2. R. L. Graham, *Complete sequences of polynomial values*, Duke Math. J. 31 (1964) 275–285.
3. J. Folkman, *On the representation of integers as sums of distinct terms from a fixed sequence*, Canad. J. Math. 18 (1966) 643–655.
4. N. Hegyvári, *On the representation of integers as sums of distinct terms from a fixed set*, Acta Arith. 92 (2000) 99–104.
5. Y.-G. Chen, *On subset sums of a fixed set*, Acta Arith. 106 (2003) 207–211.
6. E. Szemerédi, V. H. Vu, *Finite and infinite arithmetic progressions in sumsets*, Ann. of Math. 163 (2006) 1–35, Corollary 1.4; *Long arithmetic progressions in sumsets: thresholds and bounds*, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 19 (2006) 119–169, Theorem 9.4.
7. S. A. Burr, P. Erdős, *Completeness properties of perturbed sequences*, J. Number Theory 13 (1981) 446–455.
8. V. Bergelson, D. Simmons, *New examples of complete sets, with connections to a Diophantine theorem of Furstenberg*, Acta Arith. 177 (2017) 101–131.
9. S. Fan, *Strongly complete sets and a conjecture of Erdős*, arXiv:2607.14071.
10. T. Łuczak, T. Schoen, *On the maximal density of sum-free sets*, Acta Arith. 95 (2000) 225–229.
